newsitem.title: USA: Healthdyne says court denies Invacare motion.
newsitem.headline: Healthdyne says court denies Invacare motion.

text.p: Healthdyne Technologies Inc. said Friday an appeals court has denied hostile suitor Invacare Corp.'s motion for a review of a federal court ruling upholding the medical device maker's antitakeover provisions.
However, Invacare responded that the appellate court had merely decided against a quick review of the ruling, but the review will proceed after Healthdyne's July 30 shareholders meeting.

Invacare, a medical equipment manufacturer, said in a statement that it will now seek to elect only a simple majority to the Healthdyne board and it will not oppose a minority of three incumbents on the seven-member board.
Invacare said it continues to believe the provisions are illegal and it plans to pursue its appeal.

A federal judge in Atlanta last Thursday denied a request by Invacare to overturn part of Healthdyne's shareholder rights plan that allows only continuing directors to nullify the "poison pill" provisions.
"We are extremely pleased by the decision of the Court of Appeals," said Parker Petit, chairman of Healthdyne.
Petit said the company's litigation victory would have no effect on the continued exploration of possible alternatives to improve shareholder value.

"Under the Court's interpretations of Georgia law, even if Invacare's nominees are elected at the July 30 shareholders meeting, they will not be able to redeem the rights under our shareholders rights plan," said Petit.

"Given these facts, we call upon Invacare to tell our shareholders how Invacare will be in a position to buy their shares in the tender offer or to conduct its two-week so-called 'auction' of the company," he said.
Invacare said electing all seven of its nominees to the board at this time would pose a risk that the new board would be unable to sell the company.
Invacare's bid, launched in January, is valued at about $200 million. The $15-a-share offer is scheduled to expire Aug. 1, unless extended.
Healthdyne also now faces another lawsuit by Respironics Inc. alleging unlawful use of its patented technology.

Respironics said Friday that Healthdyne wilfully infringed the Pittsburgh-based company's patent on pioneering technology used in its portable Bipap medical device. One version of the device is used in ventilating a patient's lungs while another helps patients with sleep disorders.
The complaint, filed in a federal court in Pittsburgh, seeks injunctive relief and damages.
Officials of Healthdyne was not immediately available to comment.
Marietta, Ga.-based Healthdyne's stock slipped 32.81 cents to $17.375, while Invacare fell 25 cents to $23.75 on Nasdaq. Respironics was unchanged at $23.625, also on Nasdaq.
